step4.objective:
• An Ethernet interface configured as a tagged member of one or more VLANs transmits frames for those VLANs with an 802.1Q tag carrying the matching VID.
  • Frames received on a tagged interface bearing a VID for which that interface is a tagged member are classified into that VLAN and forwarded within it.
  • A single interface simultaneously holds untagged membership of one VLAN and tagged membership of one or more other VLANs, with each membership operating independently.
  • Untagged and priority-tagged frames received on an interface are classified into that interface's native/untagged VLAN.
  • Frames egressing an interface on its native/untagged VLAN leave with no VLAN tag, and the tag is removed on egress when the ingressing frame was tagged with the native VID.
  • The native/untagged VLAN of an interface is changeable, and after a change ingress classification and egress untagged transmission both follow the new native VID.
  • The same VID is configurable as a tagged member on two or more separate interfaces, and those interfaces form a single forwarding domain for that VID.
  • Tagged frames traverse a bridge between two tagged interfaces of the same VLAN with the VID, priority and payload preserved end to end.
  • Traffic in one VLAN remains isolated from interfaces that hold no membership of that VLAN, whether tagged or untagged.
  • An interface belonging to both a protocol-based VLAN and a tagged VLAN forwards each frame into the VLAN selected by the applicable classification rule, with protocol-template matching taking effect for untagged and priority-tagged frames.
  • The VID Set for a port associates each Protocol Group Identifier with a VID, and an untagged or priority-tagged frame matching a Protocol Template is assigned the corresponding VID.
  • Removal of all VLAN tagged memberships from an interface is possible, after which the interface carries only its untagged VLAN and drops or discards frames tagged with the removed VIDs.
  • An interface with no remaining VLAN membership passes no user traffic.
  • VID 0 (priority-tagged) frames received on an access/untagged interface are forwarded in the interface's untagged VLAN rather than discarded.
  • Ethernet interfaces enslaved to the global bridge default to untagged membership of VID 1 and tagged membership of all other configured VLANs in the range 2..4094.
  • Boundary VIDs (lowest and highest valid values) are configurable as tagged memberships and forward traffic identically to mid-range VIDs.
  • Configuration of a reserved or out-of-range VID on an interface is rejected with a clear error and leaves existing VLAN membership unchanged.
  • Tagging configuration for a VLAN that does not exist is either rejected or held inactive, and does not create silent forwarding for that VID.
  • Conflicting membership requests on one interface (for example two untagged VLANs) are rejected, with the prior valid state retained.
  • Frames tagged with a VID for which the ingress interface has no membership are discarded and are not leaked into any other VLAN.
  • Double-tagged or malformed 802.1Q frames arriving on a tagged interface are handled deterministically, with no forwarding into an unintended VLAN and no impact on interface stability.
  • VLAN membership and tagged/untagged status per interface are reportable, and the reported state matches the configured state.
  • The untagged set for each VLAN is reportable as the entries in the port map specifying untagged transmission.
  • Per-VLAN and per-interface frame counters increment consistently with the tagged and untagged traffic actually forwarded.
  • MAC addresses learned from tagged traffic appear in the forwarding database against the VID carried in the tag.
  • Tagging configuration persists across interface link transitions, VLAN reconfiguration and device restart, with forwarding behaviour resuming unchanged.
  • Changes to tagged membership take effect without disrupting traffic on the interface's other VLANs.
  • Rejected tagging operations and discarded frames are observable through logs or counters sufficient to distinguish a misconfiguration from a forwarding fault.

• An Ethernet interface configured as a tagged member of one or more VLANs transmits frames for those VLANs with an 802.1Q tag carrying the matching VID.
  • Frames received on a tagged interface bearing a VID for which that interface is a tagged member are classified into that VLAN and forwarded within it.
  • A single interface simultaneously holds untagged membership of one VLAN and tagged membership of one or more other VLANs, with each membership operating independently.
  • Untagged and priority-tagged frames received on an interface are classified into that interface's native/untagged VLAN.
  • Frames egressing an interface on its native/untagged VLAN leave with no VLAN tag, and the tag is removed on egress when the ingressing frame was tagged with the native VID.
  • The native/untagged VLAN of an interface is changeable, and after a change ingress classification and egress untagged transmission both follow the new native VID.
  • The same VID is configurable as a tagged member on two or more separate interfaces, and those interfaces form a single forwarding domain for that VID.
  • Tagged frames traverse a bridge between two tagged interfaces of the same VLAN with the VID, priority and payload preserved end to end.
  • Traffic in one VLAN remains isolated from interfaces that hold no membership of that VLAN, whether tagged or untagged.
  • An interface belonging to both a protocol-based VLAN and a tagged VLAN forwards each frame into the VLAN selected by the applicable classification rule, with protocol-template matching taking effect for untagged and priority-tagged frames.
  • The VID Set for a port associates each Protocol Group Identifier with a VID, and an untagged or priority-tagged frame matching a Protocol Template is assigned the corresponding VID.
  • Removal of all VLAN tagged memberships from an interface is possible, after which the interface carries only its untagged VLAN and drops or discards frames tagged with the removed VIDs.
  • An interface with no remaining VLAN membership passes no user traffic.
  • VID 0 (priority-tagged) frames received on an access/untagged interface are forwarded in the interface's untagged VLAN rather than discarded.
  • Ethernet interfaces enslaved to the global bridge default to untagged membership of VID 1 and tagged membership of all other configured VLANs in the range 2..4094.
  • Boundary VIDs (lowest and highest valid values) are configurable as tagged memberships and forward traffic identically to mid-range VIDs.
  • Configuration of a reserved or out-of-range VID on an interface is rejected with a clear error and leaves existing VLAN membership unchanged.
  • Tagging configuration for a VLAN that does not exist is either rejected or held inactive, and does not create silent forwarding for that VID.
  • Conflicting membership requests on one interface (for example two untagged VLANs) are rejected, with the prior valid state retained.
  • Frames tagged with a VID for which the ingress interface has no membership are discarded and are not leaked into any other VLAN.
  • Double-tagged or malformed 802.1Q frames arriving on a tagged interface are handled deterministically, with no forwarding into an unintended VLAN and no impact on interface stability.
  • VLAN membership and tagged/untagged status per interface are reportable, and the reported state matches the configured state.
  • The untagged set for each VLAN is reportable as the entries in the port map specifying untagged transmission.
  • Per-VLAN and per-interface frame counters increment consistently with the tagged and untagged traffic actually forwarded.
  • MAC addresses learned from tagged traffic appear in the forwarding database against the VID carried in the tag.
  • Tagging configuration persists across interface link transitions, VLAN reconfiguration and device restart, with forwarding behaviour resuming unchanged.
  • Changes to tagged membership take effect without disrupting traffic on the interface's other VLANs.
  • Rejected tagging operations and discarded frames are observable through logs or counters sufficient to distinguish a misconfiguration from a forwarding fault.

gaps: The selected ART coverage addresses the core encapsulation and classification mechanics — tagged 802.1Q frame handling on a port, the untagged-set membership that defines untagged transmission, and the protocol-based VID-assignment rules that govern how untagged and priority-tagged frames are classified. What it does not reach is the configuration-and-observability layer the TestLink and Zephyr material centres on: running-config and operational-state confirmation of tagging on an interface, the removal and cleanup path when tagging is withdrawn, and native/untagged VLAN interaction with the no-matching-VID case. Also thin are the boundary conditions — the same VID applied across two different interfaces, VID 0 tagged frames arriving on access ports, and the default global-bridge membership model in which enslaved interfaces are untagged in one VLAN and tagged across the remainder. End-to-end forwarding of tagged frames through the device is only partly represented, and the precedence between protocol-VLAN and tag-VLAN membership on a shared port has no clear automated analogue.

llm.objective_used:
• An Ethernet interface configured as a tagged member of one or more VLANs transmits frames for those VLANs with an 802.1Q tag carrying the matching VID.
  • Frames received on a tagged interface bearing a VID for which that interface is a tagged member are classified into that VLAN and forwarded within it.
  • A single interface simultaneously holds untagged membership of one VLAN and tagged membership of one or more other VLANs, with each membership operating independently.
  • Untagged and priority-tagged frames received on an interface are classified into that interface's native/untagged VLAN.
  • Frames egressing an interface on its native/untagged VLAN leave with no VLAN tag, and the tag is removed on egress when the ingressing frame was tagged with the native VID.
  • The native/untagged VLAN of an interface is changeable, and after a change ingress classification and egress untagged transmission both follow the new native VID.
  • The same VID is configurable as a tagged member on two or more separate interfaces, and those interfaces form a single forwarding domain for that VID.
  • Tagged frames traverse a bridge between two tagged interfaces of the same VLAN with the VID, priority and payload preserved end to end.
  • Traffic in one VLAN remains isolated from interfaces that hold no membership of that VLAN, whether tagged or untagged.
  • An interface belonging to both a protocol-based VLAN and a tagged VLAN forwards each frame into the VLAN selected by the applicable classification rule, with protocol-template matching taking effect for untagged and priority-tagged frames.
  • The VID Set for a port associates each Protocol Group Identifier with a VID, and an untagged or priority-tagged frame matching a Protocol Template is assigned the corresponding VID.
  • Removal of all VLAN tagged memberships from an interface is possible, after which the interface carries only its untagged VLAN and drops or discards frames tagged with the removed VIDs.
  • An interface with no remaining VLAN membership passes no user traffic.
  • VID 0 (priority-tagged) frames received on an access/untagged interface are forwarded in the interface's untagged VLAN rather than discarded.
  • Ethernet interfaces enslaved to the global bridge default to untagged membership of VID 1 and tagged membership of all other configured VLANs in the range 2..4094.
  • Boundary VIDs (lowest and highest valid values) are configurable as tagged memberships and forward traffic identically to mid-range VIDs.
  • Configuration of a reserved or out-of-range VID on an interface is rejected with a clear error and leaves existing VLAN membership unchanged.
  • Tagging configuration for a VLAN that does not exist is either rejected or held inactive, and does not create silent forwarding for that VID.
  • Conflicting membership requests on one interface (for example two untagged VLANs) are rejected, with the prior valid state retained.
  • Frames tagged with a VID for which the ingress interface has no membership are discarded and are not leaked into any other VLAN.
  • Double-tagged or malformed 802.1Q frames arriving on a tagged interface are handled deterministically, with no forwarding into an unintended VLAN and no impact on interface stability.
  • VLAN membership and tagged/untagged status per interface are reportable, and the reported state matches the configured state.
  • The untagged set for each VLAN is reportable as the entries in the port map specifying untagged transmission.
  • Per-VLAN and per-interface frame counters increment consistently with the tagged and untagged traffic actually forwarded.
  • MAC addresses learned from tagged traffic appear in the forwarding database against the VID carried in the tag.
  • Tagging configuration persists across interface link transitions, VLAN reconfiguration and device restart, with forwarding behaviour resuming unchanged.
  • Changes to tagged membership take effect without disrupting traffic on the interface's other VLANs.
  • Rejected tagging operations and discarded frames are observable through logs or counters sufficient to distinguish a misconfiguration from a forwarding fault.
